title: Paroemiae (epitome operis sub nomine Diogeniani) (e cod. Mazarinco)
author: Diogenianus of Heraclea
source: Translated by Claude from tlg0097.tlg001.1st1K-grc1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: παράκειται δὲ αὐτῇ λόγος αἶνος Αἰσώπειος, Καρικὸς αἶνος, Συβαριτικὸς λόγος, Κύπριος, Λιβυκὸς αἶνος, Μαισωνικὴ παροιμία· μάρσιπος. Αἶνος μὲν οὖν ἐστὶ κατ’ ἀνάπλασιν μυθικὴν ἀναφερόμενος ἀπὸ ἀλόγων ζώων ἢ φυτῶν ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπων παραίνεσιν. Καὶ ἀπὸ ζώων μὲν, ὡς παρ’ Ἀρχιλόχῳ, Αἶνός τις ἀνθρώπων ὅδε Ὡς ἆρ’ ἀλώπηξ κἀετὸς ξυνωνίην Ἔμιξαν. ἀπὸ δὲ φυτῶν, Ἄκουε δὴ τὸν αἶνον· ἔγ κοτε Τμώλῳ Δάφνην ἐλαίῃ νεῖκος οἱ πάλαι Λυδοὶ λέγουσι θέσθαι. Εἰκὸς δὲ καταχρηστικώτερον παρ’ Ὁμήρῳ αἶνος, ὁ μηδετέρου τούτων μετέχων, ὅτε ἐνδεικνυμένου Ὀδυσσέως χλαίνης ὡς χρῄζει ὁ Εὔμαιός φησιν, Ὦ γέρον, αἶνος μέν τοι ἀμύμων, ὃν κατέλεξας. Οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι τῶν κατειλεγμένων ὀνόματι μὲν διαφέρειν, δυνάμει δ’ εἰσὶν ἐμφερεῖς. Αἰσώπειος μὲν γὰρ λέγεται ὁ ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς Αἰσώπου πλεονάσαντος ἐν τῷ τοιούτῳ εἴδει τοῦ μύθου, οὐχ εὑρόντος, ὡς ἐν ποιητικῇ μέτρον Ἀρχεβούλειον ἢ καὶ Ἀριστοφάνειον, ἃ λέγεται οὐχ εὑρημένα ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνδρῶν, ἀλλὰ παρὰ τούτοις κατακορέστερον ἐν τῇ ποιήσει τεταγμένα.
passages.english: Related to it are the logos (tale), the Aesopic ainos (fable), the Carian ainos, the Sybaritic logos, the Cyprian, the Libyan ainos, the Maesonic proverb, [and] the marsipos. An ainos, then, is [a tale] which by mythical invention transfers [a story] from irrational animals or plants to the admonition of human beings. From animals, as in Archilochus: "There is a fable men tell, this one: how a fox and an eagle joined in partnership." From plants: "Hear now the fable: once on Tmolus, the Lydians of old say, the laurel set a quarrel with the olive." Probably in a rather looser sense, in Homer, ainos is [used of a tale] that partakes of neither of these, when, as Odysseus indicates that he needs a cloak, Eumaeus says: "Old man, blameless indeed is the ainos you have told." The others of those listed differ in name but are alike in force. For the Aesopic is so called after a man, Aesop, who made abundant use of this kind of fable, not because he invented it, just as in poetry [one speaks of] the Archebulean or the Aristophanean metre, which are said not to have been invented by these men but to have been used rather profusely by them in their poetry.
passages.notes: Μαισωνικὴ: presumably referring to Maeson, a figure of Megarian comedy. μάρσιπος (literally 'bag, pouch') appears here as an item in the list; its sense as a term for a kind of saying is unclear. ἔγ κοτε is taken as ἔν ποτε / ἐν + ποτε ('once on').

passages.original: τοῦτον γὰρ ἁλιέα τυγχάνοντα χειμῶνος θεασάμενον πολύποδα εἰπεῖν· » Εἰ μὲν ἀποδὺς κολυμβήσαιμι ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ῥιγώσω, ἐὰν δὲ μὴ λάβω τὸν πολύποδα, τῷ λιμῷ τὰ παιδί’ ἀπολῶ. « Κέχρηται δὲ τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ καὶ Τιμοκρέων ἐν μέλεσι, καὶ Σιμωνίδης δ’ αὐτοῦ μνημονεύει ἐν τῷ εἰς Ὄριλλαν Ἐπινικίῳ. Ὁ Συβαριτικὸς δὲ λέγεται εἶναι τοιοῦτος ὁποῖον Ἀριστοφάνης ἐν Σφηξὶν, ὡς ἀνδρὶ Συβαρίτῃ ἀπείρῳ ἱππικῆς ἐφ’ ἅρμα ἀναβάντι συνέβη κατενεχθέντι συντριβῆναι, φίλον δ’ αὐτῷ παρόντα φάναι τὸ ἕρδοι τις ἣν ἕκαστος εἰδείη τέχνην.
passages.english: For they say that this man, who was a fisherman, saw an octopus in winter and said: "If I strip and dive after it, I shall freeze; but if I do not catch the octopus, I shall kill my children with hunger." Timocreon also used this tale in his lyrics, and Simonides too mentions it in his Victory Ode for Orillas. The Sybaritic [tale] is said to be of the sort that Aristophanes [tells] in the Wasps: how a Sybarite man inexperienced in horsemanship mounted a chariot, was thrown out and was crushed, and a friend who was present said to him: "Let each man practise the craft he knows."
passages.notes: Ὄριλλαν: the victor Orillas is otherwise unidentified.

passages.original: Καὶ γὰρ τῷ Ἀδώνιδι ἐν Κύπρῳ τιμηθέντι ὑπὸ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν οἱ Κύπριοι ζώσας ἐνίεσαν περιστερὰς, αἱ δ’ ἀποπτᾶσαι καὶ διαφυγοῦσαι αὖθις ἀδοκήτως εἰς ἄλλην ἐμπεσοῦσαι πυρὰν διεφθάρησαν. Λιβυκὸς δὲ αἶνος ἀπὸ τοῦ ἔθνους εἰρῆσθαι λέγεται, ἀπὸ Λίβυός τινος· οἱ δὲ Κύβισαν εὑρέτην γενέσθαι τοῦ εἴδους τούτου, ὡς Αἰσχύλος διασαφεῖ, ὧδ’ ἐστὶ μύθων τῶν Λιβυκῶν τὸ κλέος.
passages.english: For in Cyprus, when Adonis was honoured by Aphrodite after his death, the Cypriots threw live doves [into the pyre]; and these flew off and escaped, but then unexpectedly fell into another pyre and perished. The Libyan fable is said to be so called from the people, [or] from a certain Libys; others [say] that Kybisas was the inventor of this kind, as Aeschylus makes clear: "Thus is the fame of the Libyan tales."
passages.notes: This passage continues an account of fable types (Sybaritic, Cyprian, Libyan) from the preface of the collection. The Adonis story illustrates the point just made, that wrongdoers meet their due later. "Into the pyre" is supplied from the sense. The name "Kybisas" (Κύβισαν, accusative) is uncertain and not identified. The Aeschylus quotation is garbled: the received line reads ὧδ' ἐστὶ μύθων τῶν Λιβυστικῶν κλέος, which is a fable about an eagle shot with an arrow fledged with its own feathers.

passages.original: Ἄνθρακες ὁ θησαυρός: ἐπὶ τῶν ἐφ’ οἷς ἤλπισαν διαψευσθέντων. Ὡς ὁ Λουκιανός· Ἄνθρακάς μοι τὸν θησαυρόν ἀπέφηνας.
passages.english: "The treasure [turned out to be] coals": said of those who have been disappointed in what they hoped for. As Lucian [says]: "You have shown me that the treasure is coals."

passages.original: Ἁλιεὺς πληγεὶς νοῦν οἴσει: ἐπὶ τῶν μετὰ τὸ ἁμαρτῆσαί τινος πράγματος συνιέντων. Ἁλιεὺς γὰρ ἁλισκομένους ἰχθῦς μετεχειρίζετο, καί ποτε πληγεὶς, Νοῦν οἴσω, φησίν· ὅμοιον δέ ἐστι τῷ παρ’ Ἡσιόδῳ, Παθὼν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω.
passages.english: "A fisherman, once stung, will get sense": said of those who understand a matter after making a mistake. For a fisherman was handling the fish he had caught, and once, when he was stung, he said, "I will get sense." It is like the line in Hesiod: "Having suffered, the fool learns."

passages.original: Ἀρχαιότερος Ἰβύκου: ἐπὶ τῶν εὐηθῶν. Οὗτος γὰρ τυραννεῖν δυνάμενος ἀπεδήμησεν.
passages.english: Older than Ibycus: [said] of simpletons. For he, though he could have been tyrant, went abroad.
passages.notes: ἀρχαιότερος is probably a corruption of ἀνοητότερος ('more foolish than Ibycus'), which better fits 'of simpletons'; translated as it stands.

passages.original: Εἰ μὴ πατὴρ ἦσθα: λείπει τὸ εἶπον ἄν σ’ οὐκ εὖ φρονεῖν. Παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.
passages.english: "If you were not [my] father": what is missing is "I would have said you were not in your right mind." [It is] in Sophocles.

passages.original: Ἐμπεδοκλέους ἔχθρα: ** Ὤμην δὲ, φησὶν [Λυσίας], ἐγὼ τοιαύτῃ φιλίᾳ συνηρμόσθαι σοι, ὥστε μηδ’ ἂν τὴν Ἐμπεδοκλέους ἔχθραν ἰσχῦσαι διαστῆσαι.
passages.english: The enmity of Empedocles: ** "I thought," says [Lysias], "that I had been joined to you in such friendship that not even the enmity of Empedocles could separate [us]."
passages.notes: The asterisks mark a lacuna in the edition. 'Enmity' alludes to Empedocles' cosmic principle of Strife.

passages.original: Ἐχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα κοὐκ ὀνήσιμα: δῆλον ἐπὶ τίνι. καὶ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.
passages.english: "The gifts of enemies are no gifts, and bring no profit": it is clear what it applies to. It is also in Sophocles.

passages.original: Λύω λέσχας: Πλάτων φησὶ λέγων ὁπόταν ἐπὶ τὰ ἔργα ἐξήρχοντο.
passages.english: "I dissolve the talk-gatherings": Plato says [this], speaking of when they went out to their work.
passages.notes: The sense is obscure, probably because of abridgement. λέσχαι are places or occasions for idle talk, and the phrase seems to mean breaking up the gossip in order to go to work. The Plato meant may be the comic poet rather than the philosopher.

passages.original: Τέλος ὅρα βίου: τοῦτο τὸ ἀπόφθεγμα Σόλων εἶπε Κροίσῳ.
passages.english: Look to the end of life: Solon said this saying to Croesus.
